About

The short version

I'm a Product Manager focused on AI and data products. My work sits where technical depth meets user empathy — I like starting from the data and ending at the human.

Right now I'm finishing graduate study at the University of Michigan across Information and Data Science, while consulting on product strategy for Purdue University's veterinary diagnostics platform and a Ross School of Business AI interview-coaching tool. On the side, I've been building QuiTam Copilot, a legaltech tool with a multi-agent AI architecture shaped by real user research.

Before grad school I spent four years at Deloitte on the Strategy & Analytics team — I built self-serve analytics platforms used by 20,000+ people, shipped some of our earliest generative-AI tooling, and ran delivery as a Scrum Master. I started my career in data science at Swiggy, building ML forecasting models that improved demand accuracy across 500+ cities.

Along the way I've published machine-learning research, built end-to-end prediction pipelines, and led user research that set product direction. It's a winding path through data, research, and product — and it's exactly what makes me useful in the room.

You're welcome to view my resume, look through some recent work below, or reach out if you'd like to talk product, data, or anything in between.

Case study · Consumer product · IPD Challenge winner

tatter.

we mend to make more memories

An app and starter toolkit that help outdoor enthusiasts repair worn and torn gear — instead of tossing it. You run a quick diagnostic, tatter. matches you to the right materials and a guided fix, and your gear gets a second chance.

RoleProduct lead — product & services TimelineSep – Dec 2024 TeamTeam Woodpecker ResultIPD Challenge winner

Overview

What it is

tatter. pairs a mobile app with a physical repair kit so people can fix their outdoor gear at home, confidently. The app diagnoses the damage and walks you through the repair; the kit makes sure you have the right materials on hand when something breaks.

It started as an Integrated Product Development challenge at Michigan, built by our team — Team Woodpecker. I led the product & services definition: the end-to-end app experience and the kit system that the rest of the strategy was built around.

The belief underneath it: every piece of worn or broken outdoor gear deserves a second chance. We took a wabi-sabi view of repair — wear is worth celebrating, and a mend is a mark of use, not a flaw to hide.

Problem space

People toss repairable gear because fixing it feels hard

Repairing your own outdoor gear is seen as daunting — it's inconvenient, it needs specific tools, and it takes know-how most people don't have. So good, expensive gear gets thrown out over a tear, a broken seam, a burn mark, or a snapped buckle. That's waste, cost, and a lost connection to gear people actually care about. The framing question we worked from:

How might we… reimagine outdoor gear repair to make it easy and sustainable for young people who want affordable, sustainable, and personalizable ways to maintain their gear — and the memories attached to it?

The timing is right: rising gear costs from tariffs and inflation, a growing sustainability and right-to-repair movement, and real evidence that hands-on, creative work is good for wellbeing. Meanwhile, the repair gap is large and measurable.

25–45Mpeople hit the repair gap each year
$4.5–12.6Bin lost gear value, replaced instead of repaired
150–300Mlbs of gear wasted annually

We grounded this in real conversations rather than assumptions. One that stuck with the team:

“I have a hunting jacket passed down from my grandfather with a burn stain on it. It's too sentimental to throw away, but I haven't fixed it because I don't know how. I can easily picture using tatter. to fix this.”

Who we serve

Outdoor people, 18–31, who'd rather mend than replace

Active, sustainability-minded young adults and professionals who own mid-to-high-quality gear, feel the rising cost of replacing it, and want affordable, personal alternatives to buying new. We shaped the product around four motivations:

Persona

The Time Keeper

Wants to repair, but is put off by the time it takes. Needs quick, convenient fixes.

Persona

The Knowledge Seeker

Willing to try, but overwhelmed by confusing instructions and too many options. Needs clear, step-by-step guidance.

Persona

The Resourceful Reuser

Motivated to cut waste and extend the life of their things. Wants accessible tools to build DIY confidence.

Persona

The Memory Saver

Hates discarding cherished gear over a small tear. Repairs to keep the memories attached to it alive.

Solution space

Diagnose, then do — with the right kit in hand

The product I designed turns “I don't know where to start” into a confident fix. You photograph the damage; the app classifies it and asks a short yes/no questionnaire to pin down the problem. From there it gives you an offline, illustrated tutorial with embedded video — and recommends the exact material kit that matches your gear. A built-in community lets people share their own mends, which is where the brand becomes a movement rather than a utility.

Photo diagnostic — snap the damage; the app classifies the issue and narrows it with a quick questionnaire.

Guided, offline tutorials — clear written steps and video, downloadable so they work with no signal on the trail.

Kit matching — the diagnostic ends on the right material kit for your gear, not a generic shopping page.

Community — a forum to post fixes, swap tips, and learn from peers (where 92% trust peer content over ads).

The needs that set our focus

I want to… figure out what's actually wrong with my gear

So that I can… know whether it's fixable before I give up on it

Example a diagnostic that narrows a leaking tent down to a seam vs. a fabric tear

I want to… follow a repair I can actually do at home

So that I can… fix it without a specialist or a return

Example step-by-step video matched to the parts already in my kit

I want to… have the right materials on hand

So that I can… repair the moment something breaks, not three weeks later

Example a kit stocked for the most common repairs for my kind of gear

The kits

Five kits to launch with

Rather than one do-everything box, the system is a small set of dual-purpose kits, each tuned to a common failure mode. Standard kits run $25–$35; larger specialized kits up to about $50. The app is free at launch so discovery stays frictionless — the kits are the business.

01

Shell + Ripstop Patch Kit

The most common damage: tears and punctures in jackets, tents, and packs, with patch weights to match the fabric.

02

Soft-Goods Stitch & Reinforce Kit

Restores worn seams, hems, and fleece — with visible-mend, sashiko-style swatches for repairs you can show off.

03

Waterproof + Seam Repair Kit

For leaks in rain shells, tents, and dry bags: seam tape, sealant, and a DWR refresh.

04

Hardware & Webbing Repair Kit

Strap and buckle failures on packs and guy-lines — replace webbing and buckles without re-buying gear.

05

Down & Insulation Repair Kit

Loft loss and small holes in puffies and sleeping bags, with patches that keep the insulation in.

Market

A small slice of a large intersection

tatter. sits where three growing markets overlap — gear repair, the outdoor category, and the DIY movement. Outdoor gear repair is the core target; even a fractional capture is a real business.

$2.13Boutdoor gear repair — the core target market
$9.7Bclothing & footwear repair, an adjacent market
~$848BDIY market — the cultural tailwind
$2.13Mannual revenue at just 0.1% of outdoor repair

Against traditional repair shops (costly, slow), brand programs (locked to one brand), bare kits (no guidance), and generic tutorials (imprecise), tatter.'s edge is the diagnostic-to-kit match: precise, brand-agnostic guidance that ends with the exact materials in hand.

Outcome

A working product that won

We shipped a working app prototype and a physical starter kit, and the project won the IPD Challenge — recognition for end-to-end product execution under real constraints: a sharp problem, a disciplined scope, and something that actually ran. The go-to-market plan laid out a path from a first 500–1,000 units toward national retail.

1stIPD Challenge — winning entry
5launch repair kits + a working app prototype
18–31target audience, repairs made approachable

Case study · LegalTech · 0→1

QuiTam
Copilot

From a pile of evidence to a court-ready case

An AI tool that helps whistleblower attorneys prepare qui tam lawsuits under the federal False Claims Act — mapping raw, messy evidence onto the legal elements a case actually needs.

RoleProduct & Strategy Timeline2025 · 24-hr build, ongoing DomainLegal · False Claims Act StackClaude API · multi-agent graph

Overview

What it is

The False Claims Act lets a private citizen — a “relator” — sue on behalf of the government when they uncover fraud against a federal program. The attorneys who take these cases have to turn raw evidence (billing records, internal emails, invoices) into a structured argument that ties each fact to the legal elements a court needs to see.

QuiTam Copilot does the first pass of that work. You hand it a bundle of documents; it hands back a structured case memo — the entities and dollar amounts, a fraud timeline, an evidence-to-law map, and an estimated damages figure — for an attorney to review and refine.

Who it's for

  • Whistleblower / qui tam attorneys — the primary user, building and filing the case.
  • The relator — the whistleblower who supplies the raw evidence.

The landscape

Adjacent tools exist — Darrow AI focuses on finding new cases, Harvey AI on general legal drafting — but none go deep on FCA complaint preparation specifically, which is exactly the gap this targets.

Problem space

Attorneys drown in pages before they can even judge a case

Preparing an FCA case means manually combing through thousands — sometimes millions — of pages to assemble a timeline and connect each piece of evidence to the law. It can take weeks per case, and that prep work is the bottleneck on how many cases a firm can take on. Meanwhile, the market this serves is enormous and growing.

$6.8Brecovered in FCA settlements in FY2025 — an all-time record
1,297new qui tam filings in a single year (+32% YoY)
~$100Bestimated lost to fraud against federal programs annually

The opportunity

No tool takes raw whistleblower evidence and maps it to the legal elements required to file. The opening: compress weeks of manual case preparation into a structured first draft — and let attorneys spend their time on judgment, not assembly.

Hypotheses

What we bet on

  • If evidence is mapped automatically to the four FCA elements — Falsity, Scienter, Materiality, Causation — an attorney can judge case strength in minutes instead of weeks.
  • A multi-agent architecture will beat a single monolithic prompt, because extraction, timeline-building, legal mapping, and damages each call for different reasoning.
  • The artifact that matters is a structured case memo with citations and a gap analysis — not a chatbot.

Solution space

Job stories

The use cases that defined what the first version had to do, and aligned the build:

I want to… upload a bundle of raw documents and get the key entities and dollar amounts pulled out

So that I can… stop manually combing billing records for the fraud signal

Example flag a clinic that billed the highest-complexity code 92% of the time against a ~40% national average

I want to… see the fraud laid out as a timeline

So that I can… show the conduct was sustained and deliberate, not accidental

Example “pattern began Jan 2022, was systemic by March, ran through Dec 2023”

I want to… see each piece of evidence mapped to the legal element it supports

So that I can… judge whether the case actually clears the bar to file

Example a strength score for Falsity, Scienter, Materiality, and Causation

I want to… get an estimated damages figure

So that I can… understand the case's scale before investing more time

Example a treble-damages estimate against the CMS fee schedule, plus per-claim penalties

Architecture

Four agents over a shared graph

A master agent coordinates four specialized agents, each leaving its work on a shared document graph the next can read. The output is a single structured memo — not a conversation.

Agent 01

Entity extractor

Pulls people, billing codes, counts, and dollar amounts from the documents and benchmarks them against national averages to flag anomalies.

Agent 02

Timeline builder

Orders the facts into a chronological story that shows whether the conduct was sustained and deliberate.

Agent 03

FCA mapper

Scores the evidence against Falsity, Scienter, Materiality, and Causation — and checks exclusion lists.

Agent 04

Damage calculator

Estimates treble damages against the fee schedule and adds per-claim civil penalties.

Outcome

A working memo, built in a day

The first version was built in a 24-hour hackathon on the Claude API and a multi-agent graph, then validated in conversations with practicing qui tam attorneys. The pitch line that stuck: TurboTax for whistleblower lawsuits — turning a pile of evidence into a court-ready draft in minutes instead of weeks.

24hrto a working MVP from scratch
4specialized agents over one shared graph
weeks→hrstarget reduction in case-prep time

Case study · Product strategy · B2B GTM

Jobago.ai

Are banks a channel for AI hiring?

A go-to-market engagement for an AI employment platform — built to answer one question: can banks be a viable institutional channel to put employment support in front of the people who need it?

RoleProduct Strategy Consultant TimelineJan – Mar 2026 MarketUnited States OutputGTM strategy & playbook

Overview

The company

Jobago.ai is an AI employment platform that uses large language models to match job seekers with opportunities. The product worked; the open question was distribution. Acquiring users one at a time, direct-to-consumer, is expensive and noisy for a service like employment support.

The hypothesis worth testing: banks already hold a trusted relationship with the exact population that benefits from employment support, and they have real incentives — community reinvestment, customer financial health, retention — to offer it. My engagement was to pressure-test that, end to end, for the US market.

Who we needed to win over

  • Job seekers — the platform's end users, reached through the bank rather than directly.
  • Bank decision-makers — the internal buyers: leaders in community programs, financial wellness, retail banking, and community reinvestment.

Problem space

A good product with an open distribution question

The strategic risk wasn't the technology — it was channel. Without a credible, repeatable way to reach users, even a strong matching product stalls. Banks were a tempting answer, but “tempting” isn't “validated.” The work had to separate the real opportunity from the appealing story: which banks, why they'd say yes, what they'd pay, and how you'd actually reach the person inside the bank who can sign.

The opportunity

If banks are a viable B2B channel, Jobago gets three things in one move: distribution at scale, borrowed trust from an institution the user already relies on, and a clearer revenue model than consumer subscriptions.

Hypotheses

What we set out to validate

  • Banks represent a viable distribution and revenue channel for employment-support services.
  • Certain bank types — large, regional, or challenger — fit far better than others, and the strategy should target the right segment rather than “banks” in general.
  • Adoption depends on a business model aligned to bank incentives — whether per-user pricing, enterprise licensing, or revenue share.
3bank segments evaluated — large, regional, challenger
6strategic deliverables, from analysis to outreach plan
B2Bchannel thesis tested against a B2C default

Solution space

The bank's side of the table

To make the value proposition real, I framed it from the buyer's point of view — what a bank actually gets out of offering this:

I want to… offer my customers a meaningful benefit beyond financial products

So that I can… deepen relationships and support their financial health

Example employment support folded into the bank's existing customer or community programs

I want to… show measurable community impact

So that I can… support reinvestment goals and the bank's standing in its market

Example helping customers find work as a reportable, repeatable program outcome

I want to… add the service without building or maintaining it myself

So that I can… move quickly and keep it off my own roadmap

Example a partnership and pricing model that fits how the bank already buys

Approach

From research to a playbook

The engagement ran from broad market scanning to a concrete, implementation-ready plan. The deliverables built on each other:

01

Market & competitive analysis

Banks already offering non-financial support tools, comparable platforms, and a map of competitors and potential collaborators.

02

Segmentation & personas

Ideal bank profiles and the key internal decision-makers to approach inside each.

03

Messaging & value prop

Positioning tuned to bank priorities — community impact, customer health, retention.

04

Business model

Pricing structure options and a revenue model weighed against bank incentives.

05

Outreach & engagement plan

Channels, innovation events, and partnership pathways to actually start conversations.

06

Executive summary

The recommended strategic direction, synthesized into a single decision-ready brief.

Outcome

A clear answer, and a way to act on it

The engagement gave Jobago what it actually needed before spending real money on a channel: clarity on whether banks are viable, a prioritized list of bank types to pursue first, messaging tailored to financial institutions, a recommended pricing and revenue structure, and a concrete outreach plan to start validating in market — rather than a tempting story left untested.
